about: The real, named 55+ and active-adult communities across Volusia and Flagler counties, and why this buyer type is a genuinely large share of the local market

hub.name: Become a Real Estate Agent in Florida

answer: This is not a small niche buyer type here. Roughly one in four Volusia County residents is 65 or older, well above both the Florida and national averages, and a new agent will run into 55-plus buyers constantly, not occasionally. The communities that come up most often include Latitude Margaritaville Daytona Beach, a large Jimmy Buffett-branded active-adult community built by Minto Communities; Cresswind DeLand, a gated, resort-style 55-plus community on Lake Winnemissett built by Kolter Homes; Pelican Bay near South Daytona, a large gated community with two golf courses that leans heavily 55-plus; and Plantation Oaks in Flagler Beach, an age-restricted manufactured home community on 115 wooded acres near Bulow Creek. Each serves a different budget and lifestyle, from resort-style new construction to lower-cost manufactured housing, and a new agent should be able to talk through the real differences rather than treat them as interchangeable.

tldr: Retirees and active adults are a large, structural part of the Volusia and Flagler real estate market, not a side niche, with roughly a quarter of Volusia County's population already 65 or older. The communities a new agent should know by name span very different price points and styles: Latitude Margaritaville Daytona Beach and Cresswind DeLand are newer, resort-style, higher-amenity options; Pelican Bay pairs golf with a gated 55-plus setting near South Daytona; and Plantation Oaks in Flagler Beach is an age-restricted manufactured home community at a meaningfully lower price point. Knowing these differences, and being ready to talk through amenity expectations and how this buyer type often finances a purchase, matters more here than in most Florida markets.
body:
Why This Buyer Type Is Not Optional Knowledge Here

In a lot of Florida markets, 55-plus buyers are one segment among several a new agent might eventually specialize in. In Volusia and Flagler counties, treating this as optional is a mistake. Roughly 25.9% of Volusia County's population is 65 or older as of 2024, well above Florida's statewide figure of about 21.8% and nearly a third higher than the national rate of roughly 18%. The county's median age, at 46.6, runs about 9% higher than the state median. That's not a niche, it's a substantial and structural part of who actually buys and sells homes here. A new agent who hasn't thought through how retiree buyers search, what they expect from a community, and how they typically finance a purchase is unprepared for a big share of the actual market, not a small corner of it.

Latitude Margaritaville Daytona Beach

Latitude Margaritaville Daytona Beach is one of the best-known names in this category regionally, built by Minto Communities, a firm with more than 45 years of master-planned development experience. It's a 55-plus active-adult community themed around the Jimmy Buffett lifestyle brand, offering new-construction single-family homes with resort-style amenities aimed at buyers who want an active, social, low-maintenance environment. It draws buyers relocating from out of state specifically for the brand recognition and the built-in social calendar that comes with a large, newer active-adult community, and it sits at a meaningfully higher price point than older or manufactured-home options in the area.

Cresswind DeLand

Cresswind DeLand, built by Kolter Homes, is a gated, resort-style 55-plus community on the shores of Lake Winnemissett in DeLand. It offers new-construction homes across a range of sizes, giving buyers who want inland, quieter DeLand over coastal Daytona Beach a comparable new-construction option in the same general category as Latitude Margaritaville. For an agent working the West Volusia side of the county, this is the community to know as the go-to answer for a retiree who specifically wants to be away from the immediate coast.

Pelican Bay

Pelican Bay, near South Daytona, is a large, gated community built around two separate 18-hole golf courses, along with a clubhouse, tennis courts, and a pool, and it's widely described as a premier 55-plus community in the area. It generally sits at a lower price point than the newest master-planned communities, which makes it a strong option for a retiree buyer who wants golf and an active clubhouse scene but doesn't need brand-new construction to get it. It also comes up on the golf-focused side of this market, so it's worth knowing both angles when talking with a buyer.

Plantation Oaks

Plantation Oaks, in Flagler Beach, is a genuinely different kind of option: an age-restricted manufactured home community spread across 115 acres of wooded, natural open space near Bulow Creek, about 7.4 miles from the Flagler Beach Fishing Pier. Amenities include an Olympic-size heated pool, a whirlpool spa, tennis and pickleball courts, and gated entry, with a lot package typically covering lawn maintenance, trash and recycling, cable, and high-speed internet in addition to the community facilities. For a retiree buyer working with a tighter budget who still wants gated, age-restricted living with real amenities, this is the kind of community that gets overlooked by agents who only know the newer, higher-priced names.

What Actually Differs Between These Communities

The real differences a new agent needs to be ready to explain aren't cosmetic. Construction age and style vary a lot, from brand-new homes at Latitude Margaritaville and Cresswind DeLand to manufactured housing at Plantation Oaks. HOA and lot-fee structures differ meaningfully too: a traditional HOA community bills dues that cover shared amenities, while a manufactured home community like Plantation Oaks typically charges lot rent that bundles in more of the day-to-day costs, like lawn care and utilities access, in a single monthly number. Amenity expectations differ as well. A buyer coming from a brand-new master-planned community expects a resort-style clubhouse and a packed activities calendar; a buyer drawn to Plantation Oaks or Pelican Bay may care more about a straightforward, well-run community at a lower monthly cost. None of these are better or worse, but they are genuinely different products, and conflating them with a buyer wastes everyone's time.

Questions Worth Asking Early, Not Assuming

New agents sometimes walk into a first conversation with a retiree buyer assuming they know what that buyer wants, and that assumption is often wrong in ways that waste everyone's time. Some 55-plus buyers specifically want a legally age-restricted community and would be unhappy to end up somewhere like Plantation Bay that only looks age-restricted. Others actively want the flexibility of a non-restricted community so grandchildren can visit for extended stays without HOA friction. Some buyers are moving here full-time and want a packed social calendar and a resort-style clubhouse; others are looking for a quieter, lower-maintenance second home and would find Latitude Margaritaville's activity level exhausting rather than appealing. A short, direct set of early questions, age restriction preference, how socially active they want the community to be, whether they're relocating full-time or part-time, and their real budget range, saves both the agent and the buyer from touring communities that were never a real match.

What an Agent Should Know About Financing This Buyer Type

Retiree buyers frequently finance differently than a typical working-age buyer. A meaningful share pay cash, often from the sale of a previous home, which changes the timeline and negotiating posture of an offer. For buyers who do finance, income can come from retirement accounts, Social Security, or pensions rather than W-2 pay stubs, which a lender documents differently but which a listing agent doesn't need to evaluate directly, that's the lender's job. What an agent should watch for instead is realistic timing: a retiree often needs to sell a home in another state before or alongside buying here, which can affect how firm an offer really is. And for manufactured home communities specifically, like Plantation Oaks, financing sometimes runs through specialized manufactured-home lenders rather than a standard mortgage, which is worth flagging early rather than assuming a buyer's pre-approval covers it.

This Spans Both Counties, Not Just One City

It's worth remembering that this buyer type isn't concentrated in a single part of the market. Daytona Beach, South Daytona, and DeLand in Volusia County each have a genuinely different named community worth knowing, and Flagler Beach in Flagler County adds its own, meaningfully lower-cost option in Plantation Oaks. A new agent shouldn't assume a retiree buyer is only interested in the coast, or only interested in staying inland, without asking. Some buyers specifically want to be near the beach and are willing to pay for it at a community like Latitude Margaritaville. Others, especially those coming from a fixed retirement income, are more focused on value and lower ongoing costs, which points toward options like Plantation Oaks or Pelican Bay regardless of which side of the county line they end up on. Asking directly, rather than assuming based on where a buyer first called from, is what actually narrows the search efficiently.

faq.q: How big is the retiree population in Volusia County, really?
faq.a: About 25.9% of Volusia County's population was 65 or older as of 2024, compared to roughly 21.8% statewide in Florida and about 18% nationally. This is a genuinely large share of the local market, not a niche.

faq.q: What is Latitude Margaritaville Daytona Beach?
faq.a: A large, Jimmy Buffett-branded 55-plus active-adult community in Daytona Beach, built by Minto Communities, offering new-construction homes with resort-style amenities.
A gated, resort-style 55-plus community built by Kolter Homes on Lake Winnemissett in DeLand, offering new-construction homes as an inland alternative to coastal Daytona Beach options.

faq.q: Is Plantation Oaks a traditional HOA community?
faq.a: No. It's an age-restricted manufactured home community in Flagler Beach that generally charges lot rent covering amenities, lawn care, and utilities access, rather than a standard HOA fee structure.

Many do, often from the sale of a previous home, which is worth understanding when evaluating how firm an offer is. Others finance normally, and manufactured-home communities specifically sometimes require a specialized manufactured-home lender rather than a standard mortgage.

faq.q: Are these communities interchangeable for a retiree buyer?
faq.a: No. They differ meaningfully in construction age, price point, fee structure, and amenities, from new-construction resort-style communities to lower-cost manufactured housing, and a new agent should understand those real differences before matching a buyer to one.
